source.title: Scaling Laws for Predicting Downstream Performance in LLMs
source.authors: Yangyi Chen; Binxuan Huang; Yi-Fan Gao; Zheng-Yang Wang; Jing-Feng Yang; Heng Ji

record.tranche_reason: The study tests power-law loss prediction and whether pre-training loss can predict downstream benchmark performance, using its own model sweeps and prediction-error evaluations. It does not reproduce the compute-optimal allocation experiment.
record.gate_note: The study also cites findings from other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Plotted results without a textual numeric value or explicit outcome are not separately extracted where a textual aggregate result is available.
record.test_reason: The study's own sweeps (43M–3B sampling models, 7B/13B targets) yield relative errors for predicting larger models' downstream performance from pre-training loss (V6). They also give domain-loss extrapolation errors under data mixing for alternative compute-to-loss forms (V2, V7). The compute-to-loss power law itself is mostly used as a tool.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the two-stage FLP (FLOPs→loss→performance) predicts 7B/13B downstream performance within 5%/10% and beats direct FLOPs-to-performance fitting. FLP-M, which uses domain-specific losses with an NN mapper, predicts 3B/7B performance across mixtures within 10% for most benchmarks and can optimise data mixtures. They note sparse sampling (TriviaQA) and FLP-M's ineffectiveness on a fixed distribution.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a power-law compute-to-pre-training-loss fit and converged checkpoints, but the principal method is a two-stage downstream-performance predictor. Models use fixed data-model ratios in the main sweep; the study does not test compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported prediction outcome depends on using average versus domain-specific loss, analytical fitting form (M1–M4), linear versus neural-network loss-to-performance mapping, data-mixture setting, sampling-model coverage, and training FLOPs/data-point density.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing ratios predicted to be optimal by FLP-M (0.01 for RACE, 0.22 for ARC) yield better 1B-model performance than the six sampled ratios.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling-law fits over data-mixture compute can select data mixtures that improve downstream performance.

record.problems: The study's primary evidence concerns downstream prediction rather than an isolated validation of loss extrapolation. The loss-fitting aggregate does not state a held-out evaluation protocol. The paper itself notes sparse sampling around TriviaQA's rapid improvement and reports that FLP-M is ineffective on a fixed pre-training distribution. Results are restricted to the reported model families, datasets, and tasks.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 2–5, 7–9, 10–16 and appendix fit curves include additional plotted results whose individual values are not stated in the text; textual aggregates and Table 3/Table 4 values are recorded instead. Other figure-only benchmark- and model-specific values are not extracted.

untested.parts: The FLOPs-to-loss fit (Eq. 1) across ~3.7e17–1e23 FLOPs is used as a tool. Its fit quality and target-loss error for the single-source models are not reported numerically. Parameters and tokens are never varied independently.
The target-loss prediction error of the single-source FLP stage is not reported; only the over-training aside (2.8%) and the mixing-setting domain loss are.
Entirely untested; a fixed token/parameter ratio is used.
Entirely untested; other modalities and regimes appear only in related work.
Exponents are not reported; parameter counting, schedule effects on exponents and compute-optimal split are untested.

missing.what: Over-training regime (~180 tokens/param): scaling laws still apply, within 2.8% error
Linear loss-to-performance fits have average R² of 93% across benchmarks
Direct FLOPs-to-performance (FP) baselines predict 7B/13B poorly; the GPT-4 form is unstable on HumanEval/TriviaQA (figure-only)
The Llama-3 two-stage NLL-to-sigmoid approach fails on this study's data points
Ablation: FLOPs input is highly inaccurate; average loss is worse than domain loss under mixing

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The main contribution is downstream prediction (V6). The FLOPs→loss power law is assumed from Kaplan/Hoffmann and fitted, but its accuracy is not reported for single-source runs. Table 4 rows compare the study's own mapper with alternatives and use actual target losses, so they isolate stage 2 only. Uncertainty is never reported.

versions.untested_parts: Tests compute-to-loss prediction, including domain-specific loss under data mixing. It does not independently vary parameters and tokens, or establish the law across several orders of magnitude with each of those held unconstrained.
Reports domain-loss prediction errors and downstream predictions for larger targets, but does not state a separate held-out evaluation protocol for the loss extrapolation itself.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation sweep or growth exponents are tested.
No controlled comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and repeated-data, fine-tuning, and transfer regimes are mentioned in related work, not tested here.
Tests downstream benchmark prediction for the stated models, tasks, and data settings; it does not establish predictability for downstream tasks generally.

Tests sensitivity to fitting forms and loss inputs, and discusses training FLOPs and sampling-data density. It does not test how parameter-count conventions affect exponents or how compute-optimal allocation exponents vary.

relationships.condition: Domain-specific loss of 3B/7B targets under general+code mixing, M4 form
relationships.reason: M4 has the lowest average error (0.014), and the text reports target errors within 2.5% for most domains (r4).
relationships.display_finding: M4 achieved the lowest average error, 0.014, with target errors within 2.5% for most domains.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Domain-specific loss of 3B/7B targets under general+code mixing, M4 form
source_check.reason: The loss-prediction results are accurate, but §5.1 includes a 3B sampling model. The 3B/7B targets do not establish V2's extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger than the largest fitting run; Table 1 gives 9.63212E+21 FLOPs for 3B and 5.09208E+22 for 7B.

relationships.reason: Error depends on fit form, from 0.029 for the total-compute law to 0.014 for M4. The single total-compute law errs on the code domain and is unstable across ratios (r1–r4).
relationships.display_finding: Prediction error falls from 0.029 for the total-compute law to 0.014 for M4, while the total-compute law mispredicts code loss and varies across mixture ratios.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: §6.2 and Table 3 show fit-form dependence: average errors are 0.029, 0.026, 0.017 and 0.014. The total-compute form has high code-domain errors and instability across mixing ratios.

relationships.condition: FLP (average loss to linear mapping), 7B/13B targets from ≤3B sampling models, and 13B MMLU
relationships.reason: Relative errors are within 5% (7B) and 10% (13B) across all benchmarks, and 3.54% on MMLU (r5–r7).
relationships.display_finding: Relative prediction errors stay within 5% for 7B models and 10% for 13B models across all benchmarks, with 3.54% error on 13B MMLU.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: FLP (average loss to linear mapping), 7B/13B targets from ≤3B sampling models, and 13B MMLU
source_check.reason: §3.4 reports errors within 5% and 10% for 7B and 13B. Appendix B reports 3.54% on 13B MMLU using 7B intermediate checkpoints, a separate sampling condition.

relationships.condition: FLP-M on 3B/7B targets across code-mixing ratios, most benchmarks, and linear/NN mappers in Table 4 except HumanEval
relationships.reason: Errors are within 10% for most benchmarks (r8, r9). Table 4 errors are 0.4–9.1% for NN and 2.5–7.8% for linear on most tasks (r16, r17, r20, r22–r29).
relationships.display_finding: Most benchmark errors stay within 10%, with neural-network mapping errors of 0.4–9.1% and linear mapping errors of 2.5–7.8% on most tasks other than HumanEval.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: FLP-M on 3B/7B targets across code-mixing ratios, most benchmarks, and linear/NN mappers in Table 4 except HumanEval
source_check.reason: §5.4 supports the most-benchmarks claim. The linked Table 4 cells show low mapping errors; these use actual target losses. Linear ARC is excluded from the linked successful rows and belongs with the alternative-mapper limitations.

relationships.condition: TriviaQA and HumanEval under FLP-M, and with alternative mappers
relationships.reason: TriviaQA error is 20–30%, attributed to sparse sampling across a jump (r10). HumanEval errors are 12–18.6% for all mappers. The automated mapper reaches 13–17% on BBH, ARC and TriviaQA (r15, r18, r19, r21, r30–r32).
relationships.display_finding: TriviaQA prediction error reached 20–30% with sparse sampling across a jump, HumanEval errors were 12–18.6% across mappers, and the automated mapper had 13–17% errors on BBH, ARC and TriviaQA.
